issues.issue: The paragraph is headed "Entire Agreement" but its text only supersedes prior agreements "containing general terms and conditions for repurchase transactions," and contains no integration language excluding other understandings. What earlier or collateral agreements survive is left open by the mismatch between heading and words.

The blanket prohibition on assigning "rights and obligations" and the nullity sanction cannot be squared with Paragraph 15(b), which expressly permits a party to assign or charge its interest in sums payable under Paragraph 11. The scope of the bar has to be read down by reference to that later subparagraph.

Termination on written notice is subject to the Agreement remaining "applicable to any Transactions then outstanding," without saying whether demand Transactions or the automatic rollover of Transactions is thereby preserved. How long the Agreement survives notice is unstated.

This carve-out permits assignment or charging of sums payable under Paragraph 11, which qualifies Paragraph 15(a)'s rule that any assignment of rights without consent is "null and void." The boundary between the prohibition and the carve-out is not drawn.

The requirement that no modification, waiver or consent be effective unless in a writing executed by both parties stands against Paragraph 3(a), which allows Transactions to be agreed orally, and Paragraph 13, which allows notices and demands to be made orally. Whether oral dealings can vary performance obligations turns on reconciling these provisions.

Seller is deemed to represent that there has been "no material adverse change" in its financial condition, a term the Agreement nowhere defines or measures. Because an incorrect representation is an Event of Default under Paragraph 11(vi), the undefined standard carries default consequences.

The characterization is self-qualifying — each Transaction is a "repurchase agreement" "except insofar as the type of Securities ... or the term ... would render such definition inapplicable" — so the provision concedes the very question it purports to settle. Whether a given mortgage-backed Transaction falls inside the statutory definition is left to be litigated.

Annex I recites that it is issued pursuant to a Master Repurchase Agreement "dated as of September 20, 1997," while the Agreement it is annexed to is dated as of September 20, 1998. The mis-recital puts in issue which instrument these Supplemental Terms attach to.

Annex I.2 states that "[a]s set forth in Paragraph 6" the parties intend all Transactions to be sales and purchases, but Paragraph 6 also deems a pledge and grants a security interest in the event Transactions are treated as loans. The Annex recites only half of the paragraph it invokes.

This amendment makes a Confirmation prevail over the Agreement, reversing the final sentence of Paragraph 3(b) as printed in the body of the instrument. Which sentence governs a Confirmation term that alters margin or default mechanics is a direct conflict between the two texts.

The default interest undertaking is set at "the LIBOR Rate as it fluctuates from day to day plus 1%," but "LIBOR Rate" (and the capitalized "Business Day") is nowhere defined, with no tenor, screen page or fixing time specified. The rate payable on a delayed remittance cannot be computed from the words used.

The tax-documentation covenant extends to "any form or document that may be required or reasonably requested," an open-ended obligation whose breach forfeits the gross-up. Neither the class of documents nor what makes a request reasonable is bounded.

A Tax Event notice is "treated as a demand pursuant to paragraph 3(c)," but Paragraph 3(c) governs only Transactions terminable on demand, so its application to a fixed-term Transaction is not provided for. How a fixed-term Transaction is unwound on a Tax Event has to be worked out between the two provisions.

Limb (iii) speaks of "the party" being required to pay "the other party" an additional amount as a result of a consolidation or merger "of such other party by such other party," so which party's corporate transaction triggers the Tax Event is ambiguous on the face of the sentence. Limb (ii) compounds this by resting on a "substantial likelihood" that is nowhere measured.

The stamp-tax indemnity is triggered when a party "becomes a Defaulting Party under this Agreement," a capitalized term the Agreement never defines — Paragraph 11 uses only the lower-case "defaulting party." Whether the indemnity attaches on an Event of Default or on some other status is unstated.

"Stamp Tax" is defined by a list closing with "or similar tax," leaving the reach of the indemnity beyond stamp, registration and documentation taxes undefined. Whether a foreign transfer levy is "similar" is not answerable from the definition.

"Tax" is defined to include any "levy, impost, duty, charge, assessment or fee of any nature" imposed in respect of any payment, a catch-all with no boundary against ordinary transaction charges. The gross-up obligation in 4(b) rides entirely on that open definition.

This paragraph applies "[n]otwithstanding any provision contained in this Agreement or in any additional terms or conditions contained in the Confirmation," while Annex I.3 provides that a Confirmation prevails over the Agreement. The two priority rules point in opposite directions where a Confirmation covers ineligible Securities.

This subparagraph requires each Transaction to be confirmed by Credit Suisse First Boston Corporation as Agent, whereas Paragraph 3(b) requires Buyer or Seller (or both) to deliver the Confirmation. Whose confirmation is the operative "Confirmation" for purposes of the conclusive-evidence rule is left in conflict.

The Agent's duty to issue "all required confirmations and statements" is keyed to "Rule 15c3-1 under the Exchange Act," which is the net capital rule and has nothing to do with confirmations. The mis-citation leaves the confirmation obligation without an identifiable standard.

The Agent is given "no responsibility or personal liability" and "otherwise no liability," yet the same sentence preserves liability for gross negligence, willful misconduct and securities-law non-compliance. The scope left to the exculpation after the carve-outs, and the fact that the whole of Annex I.6 applies only if Thornburg is a U.S. non-broker-dealer, is unresolved on these words.

Annex I.7 makes Credit Suisse First Boston (Hong Kong) Limited or an affiliate the pricing source when no vendor price is available, displacing Paragraph 2(j)'s requirement of "a generally recognized source agreed to by the parties" and imposing no good-faith or commercial-reasonableness standard on that self-interested valuation. The two provisions give different answers to who values illiquid Securities for margin purposes.

The substituted Paragraph 12 extends the single-relationship acknowledgment to "all transactions and agreements between them," so a default under an unrelated agreement becomes an Event of Default hereunder. That cannot be squared with Paragraph 11's closed list of Events of Default.

The setoff right reaches "any other amounts or obligations owing in respect of any other agreement or transaction whatsoever," an unbounded phrase with no limit to the parties' repo dealings or to matured obligations. What may be set off, and when, is not fixed by these words.

This grant of a security interest in all property transferred "pursuant to this Agreement or otherwise" sits against Paragraph 6, which deems a security interest to arise only if Transactions are recharacterized as loans, and against Annex I.2's sale intent. Whether Purchased Securities are held outright or as collateral cannot be answered without reconciling them.

The notice must be given "at or prior to 10:00 am (New York Time) on such business day," but no business day has been identified earlier in the sentence, so the deadline has no antecedent. The consequence of Buyer's refusal — that Buyer "shall offer Seller the right to terminate" — likewise fixes no terms or deadline for that offer.

The costs and "the loss incurred by Buyer" on a substitution or termination are "solely determined and calculated by Buyer in good faith," with no methodology, verification or dispute mechanism. What Seller owes therefore depends entirely on the counterparty's own unreviewed calculation.

This absolute bar on indirect, incidental, special and consequential loss cannot be squared with Paragraph 11(g), which makes the defaulting party liable for the cost of entering into replacement transactions and entering into or terminating hedge transactions and for "any other loss ... directly arising" from a default. Whether hedge-unwind and replacement damages survive the exclusion is a direct conflict.

The submission is to "EXCLUSIVE JURISDICTION" of New York courts but only "SOLELY FOR THE PURPOSE OF ANY SUIT ... BROUGHT TO ENFORCE ITS OBLIGATIONS HEREUNDER OR RELATING IN ANY WAY TO THIS AGREEMENT." Whether the clause forecloses suit elsewhere — including tort or bankruptcy-related claims brought in another district — is not settled by that qualified wording.

The statement that the Agreement "covers all Transactions in effect as of the date hereof" applies its terms retroactively to Transactions made under whatever arrangements preceded it, which Paragraph 14 purports to supersede. Which terms governed those pre-existing Transactions is a question only the two provisions together raise.
